lead: A failure theory turns a complex stress state into one number, called an equivalent stress, and compares it with the yield strength of the material. Without it, a shaft under bending and torsion would need a separate test for every combination of loads. The theory gives a factor of safety for design. Brittle parts such as cast iron brackets use Rankine; ductile parts such as mild steel shafts use Tresca or von Mises. The calculation starts from the principal stresses.
prereq: You need: principal stresses from 2.4, stress state labels from 2.1, and factor of safety from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Yield strength, factor of safety and equivalent stress

blocks.text: Yield strength σ<sub>Y</sub> is the stress at which a standard uniaxial tensile specimen begins to deform permanently. It carries units of MPa. For a design, the working stress must stay below σ<sub>Y</sub> by a margin. The factor of safety FS is the ratio FS = σ<sub>Y</sub> / σ<sub>working</sub>. A value FS = 2 means the part carries twice the load it is expected to see before yielding. For brittle materials the limiting stress is the ultimate strength: σ<sub>ut</sub> in tension and σ<sub>uc</sub> in compression. In the formulas below, use that limiting strength in place of σ<sub>Y</sub> when the material is brittle.

At a point inside a machine part, the stress state is not uniaxial. It has three principal stresses, ordered σ<sub>1</sub> ≥ σ<sub>2</sub> ≥ σ<sub>3</sub>, with tension positive. A failure theory defines an equivalent stress σ<sub>eq</sub> from these three numbers. Yielding is predicted when σ<sub>eq</sub> = σ<sub>Y</sub>. For design, the condition is σ<sub>eq</sub> ≤ σ<sub>Y</sub> / FS.

blocks.where: σ<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent stress from the chosen theory (MPa); σ<sub>Y</sub> is yield strength (MPa); FS is factor of safety (dimensionless).

blocks.text: The theory is a model, not a new material property. Each theory is a statement about which stress measure causes failure: a large normal stress, a large shear stress, or a large change of shape.

Rankine theory, also called the maximum principal stress theory, says failure occurs when the largest principal stress reaches the limiting strength. For brittle materials that limiting strength is the ultimate strength: σ<sub>ut</sub> when the largest principal stress is tensile, σ<sub>uc</sub> when it is compressive. For ductile materials in this theory the limiting strength is σ<sub>Y</sub>. For a general stress state, use the largest absolute value. The condition is max(|σ<sub>1</sub>|, |σ<sub>2</sub>|, |σ<sub>3</sub>|) = σ<sub>L</sub> / FS, where σ<sub>L</sub> is σ<sub>ut</sub>, σ<sub>uc</sub> or σ<sub>Y</sub> as above. Use Rankine for brittle materials: cast iron, ceramics, concrete. A cast iron bracket cracks on the plane of maximum tension; it does not yield first. Rankine ignores shear, so it is unsafe for ductile metals. Under pure shear, σ<sub>1</sub> = τ, σ<sub>3</sub> = −τ, σ<sub>2</sub> = 0. Rankine predicts failure at τ = σ<sub>Y</sub>, but mild steel yields near 0.5σ<sub>Y</sub>.

Tresca theory, also called the maximum shear stress theory, says failure occurs when the maximum shear stress reaches the shear yield strength, σ<sub>Y</sub>/2. The maximum shear is τ<sub>max</sub> = (σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>) / 2. The yield condition is σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = σ<sub>Y</sub>. The factor of safety is FS = σ<sub>Y</sub> / (σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>). Use Tresca for ductile materials. It is conservative: it predicts yield earlier than tests in most combined stress states. It is simple for design checks.

In plane stress one principal stress is zero. Sort it into the set before taking σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>. If both in-plane principal stresses are positive, then σ<sub>3</sub> = 0, and σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> = σ<sub>1</sub>, not σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>.

sections.h3: von Mises and the yield surfaces

blocks.text: The von Mises equivalent stress is σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(0.5[(σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup> + (σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2</sup> + (σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup>]). Yielding is predicted when σ<sub>vm</sub> = σ<sub>Y</sub>, and FS = σ<sub>Y</sub> / σ<sub>vm</sub>. This is the maximum distortion energy theory. Hydrostatic stress σ<sub>1</sub> = σ<sub>2</sub> = σ<sub>3</sub> = p gives σ<sub>vm</sub> = 0, so deep sea pressure alone does not yield a ductile metal. Only the change of shape, called distortion, stores the energy that causes yield.

In plane stress with σ<sub>3</sub> = 0, the formula becomes σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(σ<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>). In terms of the given components, σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(σ<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> − σ<sub>x</sub>σ<sub>y</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> + 3τ<sub>xy</sub><sup>2</sup>).

Plot σ<sub>1</sub> against σ<sub>2</sub> for plane stress with σ<sub>3</sub> = 0. Tresca gives a hexagon: six straight lines where the largest stress difference equals σ<sub>Y</sub>. von Mises gives an ellipse through the hexagon's corners. The ellipse is outside the hexagon, so von Mises allows a slightly higher load before yield. Under pure shear, Tresca predicts τ = 0.5σ<sub>Y</sub>; von Mises predicts τ = σ<sub>Y</sub>/√3 ≈ 0.577σ<sub>Y</sub>. Tests on ductile steels lie closer to von Mises. Use Rankine for brittle, Tresca for a safe ductile design, and von Mises for an accurate ductile check.

spec.title: Failure theory comparison
spec.aria: A flow from given stresses to sorted principal stresses, then to factors of safety by Rankine, Tresca and von Mises.

examples.question: A plane stress point has σx = 100 MPa, σy = −50 MPa and τxy = 40 MPa. Yield strength is σY = 250 MPa. Find the principal stresses and the factor of safety by Rankine, Tresca and von Mises.
steps: Average normal stress: σavg = (σx + σy) / 2 = (100 − 50) / 2 = 25 MPa.

Radius of the principal stress circle: R = √[((σx − σy) / 2)<sup>2</sup> + τxy<sup>2</sup>] = √[(150 / 2)<sup>2</sup> + 40<sup>2</sup>] = √(75<sup>2</sup> + 40<sup>2</sup>) = √(5625 + 1600) = √7225 = 85 MPa.
In-plane principal stresses: σa = σavg + R = 25 + 85 = 110 MPa and σb = σavg − R = 25 − 85 = −60 MPa.
Add the zero out-of-plane stress and sort: σ1 = 110 MPa, σ2 = 0 MPa, σ3 = −60 MPa.
Rankine: largest absolute principal stress = 110 MPa. FS = σY / 110 = 250 / 110 = 2.27.
examples.answer: The principal stresses are 110, 0 and −60 MPa. The factors of safety are 2.27 by Rankine, 1.47 by Tresca and 1.67 by von Mises; Tresca is the most conservative.
examples.check:
import math
sx = 100.0
sy = -50.0
txy = 40.0
sY = 250.0
avg = (sx + sy) / 2.0
R = math.hypot((sx - sy) / 2.0, txy)
p1 = avg + R
p2 = avg - R
s1 = max(p1, p2, 0.0)
s3 = min(p1, p2, 0.0)
s2 = p1 + p2 + 0.0 - s1 - s3
print(round(s1, 2))
print(round(s2, 2))
print(round(s3, 2))
print(round(sY / max(abs(s1), abs(s2), abs(s3)), 2))
print(round(sY / (s1 - s3), 2))
svm = math.sqrt(0.5 * ((s1 - s2) ** 2 + (s2 - s3) ** 2 + (s3 - s1) ** 2))
print(round(svm, 2))
print(round(sY / svm, 2))

traps: Using σ<sub>x</sub> and σ<sub>y</sub> in Tresca or von Mises without care. Tresca needs the principal stresses, with σ<sub>3</sub> = 0 included in plane stress, because it uses σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>. von Mises may be found from the components only if τ<sub>xy</sub> is kept: σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(σ<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> − σ<sub>x</sub>σ<sub>y</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> + 3τ<sub>xy</sub><sup>2</sup>). Dropping τ<sub>xy</sub> or using σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub> where σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> is required gives a wrong answer.
Forgetting to sort the principal stresses. Tresca always uses σ1 − σ3, the largest minus the smallest.
Using Rankine for ductile steel or Tresca for cast iron. Rankine is for brittle materials; Tresca and von Mises are for ductile materials.
Inverting the factor of safety. FS = σY / σeq, not σeq / σY.
Dropping the negative sign on a compressive principal stress. It changes σ1 − σ3 and the squared differences in von Mises.

quiz.q: Define yield strength σY and factor of safety FS.
quiz.a: σY is the uniaxial stress at which permanent deformation begins, in MPa. FS is the ratio of σY to the working equivalent stress, dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does a hydrostatic stress state not cause von Mises yield?
quiz.a: For σ1 = σ2 = σ3 = p, each difference in the von Mises formula is zero, so σvm = 0. Hydrostatic stress changes volume but does not distort shape, and von Mises depends on distortion energy.

quiz.q: A point has σ1 = 120 MPa, σ2 = 40 MPa, σ3 = −20 MPa. Yield strength is 240 MPa. Find the Tresca factor of safety.
For the same point, find the von Mises equivalent stress and factor of safety.
Compare the Tresca and von Mises yield surfaces in plane stress and say which is conservative.
quiz.a: Tresca is a hexagon and von Mises is an ellipse through its corners. The ellipse lies outside the hexagon, so Tresca predicts yield at a lower stress and is conservative.

quiz.q: Under pure shear τ, what does Rankine predict for yield, and what does Tresca predict?
quiz.a: Rankine gives σ1 = τ and predicts yield at τ = σY. Tresca gives σ1 − σ3 = 2τ and predicts yield at τ = 0.5σY. Rankine overestimates the shear strength of ductile metals.

quiz.q: Which failure theory is used for a cast iron bracket and why?
quiz.a: Rankine, because cast iron is brittle and fails by cracking under maximum principal tensile stress, not by shear yielding.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element software reports von Mises stress by default for ductile metals, and design codes often allow Tresca as a conservative check. Anisotropic sheet metals need Hill's yield criterion, and soils and concrete need pressure-dependent models such as Drucker-Prager. Search for ASME pressure vessel allowable stress, von Mises yield criterion, and Hill anisotropic yield for the next step.
